verses.text: For three years there was no war between Syria and Israel.
In the third year King Jehoshaphat of Judah went down to visit the king of Israel.
The king of Israel asked his officials, “You know Ramoth Gilead belongs to us, don't you? Why are we sitting here instead of taking it back from the king of Syria?”
Then he asked Jehoshaphat, “Will you go with me to fight at Ramoth Gilead?” Jehoshaphat answered, “I'm with you. My people are your people, and my horses are your horses.”
But Jehoshaphat added, “Please ask what the LORD has to say first.”
So the king of Israel gathered about four hundred prophets and asked them, “Should I go to war against Ramoth Gilead or hold back?” They said, “Go. The Lord will hand it over to the king.”
Jehoshaphat asked, “Isn't there another prophet of the LORD here we can ask?”

The king of Israel answered, “There's still one man we can ask for the LORD's word, Micaiah son of Imlah. But I hate him. He never prophesies anything good about me, only disaster.” Jehoshaphat said, “The king shouldn't talk like that.”
Then the king of Israel called an officer and said, “Get Micaiah son of Imlah here quickly.”
The king of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah were sitting on their thrones in royal robes in an open area at the gate of Samaria. All the prophets were prophesying before them.
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah had made himself iron horns. He said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘With these you'll drive back the Syrians until they're destroyed.’”
All the other prophets gave the same message: “Go up to Ramoth Gilead and win! The LORD will hand it over to the king.”
The messenger who went to get Micaiah told him, “All the prophets are telling the king the same good news. Please agree with them and give him good news too.”
Micaiah replied, “As surely as the LORD lives, I'll say only what the LORD tells me.”
When Micaiah came in, the king asked him, “Should we go to war at Ramoth Gilead or hold back?” Micaiah answered, “Go and win! The LORD will hand it over to the king.”
The king said, “How many times do I have to make you swear to tell me only the truth in the LORD's name?”
Micaiah answered, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains like sheep without a shepherd. The LORD said, ‘These people have no master. Let each one go home in peace.’”
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Didn't I tell you? He never prophesies good for me, only disaster.”
Micaiah said, “Then hear the LORD's word. I saw the LORD sitting on his throne with the whole army of heaven standing on his right and his left.
The LORD asked, ‘Who will lure Ahab into going up to Ramoth Gilead so he falls there?’ One suggested one thing and another suggested something else.
Then a spirit stepped forward, stood before the LORD, and said, ‘I'll lure him.’
‘How?’ the LORD asked. The spirit said, ‘I'll go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.’ The LORD said, ‘You'll lure him and succeed. Go do it.’
So the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouths of all these prophets of yours. The LORD has declared disaster for you.”
Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah went up and slapped Micaiah across the cheek. “Which way did the LORD's Spirit go when he left me to speak to you?” he asked.
Micaiah answered, “You'll find out the day you go into an inner room to hide.”
The king of Israel ordered, “Take Micaiah back to Amon the city governor and Joash the king's son.
Tell them the king says, ‘Put this man in prison. Give him only bread and water to keep him alive until I return safely.’”
Micaiah answered, “If you come back safely, the LORD hasn't spoken through me.” Then he called out, “Listen to this, all of you!”
So the king of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah went to Ramoth Gilead.
The king of Israel told Jehoshaphat, “I'll go into battle in disguise, but you wear your royal robes.” So he disguised himself and went into battle.
Meanwhile the king of Syria had ordered his thirty-two chariot commanders, “Don't fight anyone, great or small, except the king of Israel.”
When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they thought, “That must be the king of Israel!” They turned toward him to fight, and Jehoshaphat cried out.
When they realized he wasn't the king of Israel, they stopped chasing him.
But a man shot an arrow at random and hit the king of Israel between the joints of his armor. The king told his chariot driver, “Turn around and get me out of the battle. I'm badly wounded.”
The fighting grew fiercer that day. The king was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians, and he died that evening. Blood from his wound had run into the bottom of the chariot.
Around sunset a shout went through the army: “Everyone back to your town! Everyone back to your own land!”
The king died, and they took him back to Samaria and buried him there.
They washed his chariot at the pool of Samaria, where the prostitutes bathed, and the dogs licked up his blood, just as the LORD had said.
The rest of Ahab's acts, everything he did, the ivory palace he built, and all the towns he built are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Ahab died and joined his ancestors, and his son Ahaziah became king in his place.
Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king of Judah in the fourth year of King Ahab's reign over Israel.
Jehoshaphat was thirty-five when he became king, and he ruled for twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother was Azubah daughter of Shilhi.
He followed the ways of his father Asa and didn't turn away from them. He did what was right in the LORD's eyes. But the high places remained, and people still sacrificed and burned incense there.
Jehoshaphat made peace with the king of Israel.
The rest of Jehoshaphat's acts, the power he showed, and his wars are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
He drove out the male shrine prostitutes who had remained in the land after the reign of his father Asa.
There was no king in Edom at that time. A deputy ruled there.
Jehoshaphat built ships of Tarshish to sail to Ophir for gold. They never went because they were wrecked at Ezion Geber.
Ahaziah son of Ahab told Jehoshaphat, “Let my men sail with yours.” Jehoshaphat refused.
Jehoshaphat died and joined his ancestors. He was buried with them in the city of his ancestor David, and his son Jehoram became king in his place.
Ahab's son Ahaziah became king over Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of King Jehoshaphat's reign over Judah. He ruled Israel for two years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight. He followed the ways of his father and mother and of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had led Israel into sin.
He served and worshiped Baal and provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger, just as his father had done in every way.
